en: The Fifth [Chapter]: Master Zhizhe of Tiantai of the Sui Dynasty Expounds;
Recorded by His Disciple Guanding.
Regarding "Discerning the Penetrated and the Blocked": this is also called "knowing gain and loss," and it is also called "knowing characters and non-characters."
As above, the universal refutation of dharmas should lead one to penetrate non-arising.
If one does not enter [this state],
one will inevitably pursue gain and loss and remain mired in right and wrong;
thus, one must not form a fixed interpretation.
Why is this? If one’s attachment to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness is the same as that of the non-Buddhists,
it should be thoroughly refuted by means of the four propositions.
The refuter can cause the crowd to pass through just as the refuted object is demolished; however,
if one does not maintain the wisdom that contemplates emptiness,
then the refuter will not be able to demolish the refuted object as intended.
It is simply a matter of breaking through obstructions while preserving what is permeable—
just as one removes the film to nurture the pearl, or defeats the enemy to protect the general. If that is so, [then...]
That great guide, being well-acquainted with the passages and obstructions, leads the multitude and is able to pass through five hundred yojanas. (The old translation says: "The Great Guide."
In the sixth stage, the exhaustion of the afflictions of view and thought constitutes three hundred;
in the seventh and eighth stages, four hundred;
and in the ninth and tenth stages, five hundred.
This interpretation contradicts the *Vyākhyā*.
The treatise takes the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) as four hundred;
the paths of the two vehicles are not the seventh or eighth stages (*bhūmi*).
If one takes the three realms as three hundred and adds the two types of birth and death—
those of skillful means and those of causal conditions— as five hundred,
then the meaning of "comprehensive" is not fully exhausted.
Furthermore, to which hundred [categories] do those with subsequent birth-and-death and those without subsequent birth-and-death belong?
The followers of the *Dìchí* (Earth-Stage) school take the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the ten stages as five hundred.
This contradicts the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
In the Lotus Sūtra, a conjured city is created at a distance of three hundred yojanas;
here, however, it is created at a distance of two hundred yojanas.
Furthermore, there are those who interpret the three realms as constituting the "three hundred."
The two vehicles together constitute five hundred [yojanas].
This interpretation involves three errors:
first, it posits that the city of transformation is established outside the triple world.
Why is it that the followers of the two vehicles, having emerged from outside the triple world, do not enter the city?
Why must they travel further for four or five hundred *yojanas*, beyond which there is no more transformed city?
What is it that they enter such that they are called followers of the Two Vehicles?
It is because the illusory city has been extinguished that they are finally able to advance;
yet before the city has even been extinguished, they suddenly advance four hundred or five hundred [yojanas].
Third, the two vehicles enter the conjured city together.
Why is it that for the śrāvakas there are four hundred [stages] and for the pratyekabuddhas five hundred?
Some take the afflictions of the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*) to constitute the five hundred.
However, since the followers of the Two Vehicles have already severed the four abodes (*catvāra āśrayāḥ*),
the conjured city should be established four hundred *yojanas* away.
Some take the severing of the afflictions of the three realms (*tridhātu-kleśa*) to be three hundred.
To say that the *rajas* [defilements] constitute four hundred and ignorance constitutes five hundred is also not correct.
The *yojana* is originally a metaphor for afflictions (*kleśa*).
Why is it that [the number of] views (*dṛṣṭi*) is not counted when they are many,
yet thoughts (*vitarka*)— though few— are counted as three hundred?
The name and meaning of this originate fundamentally from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, five hundred [disciples] are cited as the basis for the analogy;
this is combined with the guide who perceives the perilous path of birth and death.
One should clarify the five hundred [monks] in three sections;
this is how one understands the sutra.
The first concerns the locus of birth and death.
Second, regarding afflictions;
third, regarding wisdom.
The explanations of various masters—whether comprehensive or partial, active or quiescent—do not accord with the text.
It is like using a single-pronged spoon to open a three-pronged lock.

The first school establishes the city of transformation based on the four hundred [stages] by way of the general positions; the second school, concerning birth and death, demarcates two types within the wilderness.
The first school holds that the provisional transformation city is established within the boundaries;
the second school maintains that the ultimate reality is revealed directly without waiting for the opening of the provisional means.
Such are the errors of these teachers.
What is the intention of the *Śāstra*?
The treatise contains two textual versions.
In the first, the Two Vehicles are treated as four hundred [verses] and the text stops there, rather than making it five hundred.
The subsequent passage treats the two vehicles as one hundred;
here, we reconcile this.
The treatise clarifies the underlying intention.
The Daoists take the ultimate truth as their pinnacle;
having transcended the three realms, they have not yet destroyed the "transformed city" but merely enter nirvana—
this is precisely what they point to as nirvana.
This makes four hundred ears.
Furthermore, regarding the designation of the two vehicles as one hundred,
this further clarifies that Bodhisattvas who emerge from the provisional emerge from emptiness to emerge into the provisional.
Taking non-nirvana as one hundred,
entering the three realms as three hundred—
interpret the text in this manner.
There is no contradiction with the sūtras or śāstras.
Now, regarding the clarification of the "five hundred yojanas":
first, it refers to the location of saṃsāra.
That is to say, the retributions of the three realms constitute three hundred [yojanas].
The land of skillful means with remainder and the land of true reward without obstruction constitute five hundred yojanas of location.
Next, regarding the afflictions:
That is to say, the delusions of seeing the truths (satyadarśana-heya) constitute one hundred;
the five lower-tier divisions constitute two hundred;
and the five upper-tier divisions constitute three hundred.
The "dust-sands" constitute four hundred;
ignorance constitutes five hundred.
Next, regarding the wisdom of contemplation:
The wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness knows three hundred;
the wisdom of the contemplation of the provisional knows four hundred;
the wisdom of the contemplation of the middle knows five hundred.
This accords with the text and avoids the errors of the aforementioned masters.
Furthermore, the masters' assessments of the stages are far removed from reality;
practitioners at the initial stage have not yet even severed the afflictions of false views.
By what means is one able to traverse five hundred *yojanas*?
Now, in discussing the *yojana*, there are cases where it extends horizontally through open or obstructed spaces, and cases where it extends vertically through open or obstructed spaces.
The horizontal [obstructions] consist of three dharmas in brief:
suffering and its origin constitute the blockage, while the path and cessation constitute the passage.
Ignorance and the twelve links of dependent origination constitute the blockage.
The cessation of ignorance constitutes the opening;
the six obscurations covering the mind constitute the blockage;
the six perfections constitute the opening.

Regarding "vertically penetrating the obstructed and the unobstructed": the delusions of views and thoughts, as well as birth-and-death within the realm of segmented existence, constitute the obstruction;
the contemplation that enters emptiness from the conventional constitutes the penetration.
Lack of knowledge regarding skillful means and birth-and-death constitute an obstruction;
entering the contemplation of the provisional from emptiness constitutes a passage.
Ignorance as a causal condition and birth-and-death, etc., constitute an obstruction.
The Middle Way and right contemplation constitute the "penetration.
Now, we shall examine penetration and obstruction through horizontal weaving and vertical inspection.
For example, entering emptiness from the conventional breaks through all views and afflictions.
The single and the multiple are fully present within the ineffable and equal vision;
there are eighty-one thoughts (cetanā) in nine times nine.
Such delusions as these are, by their very nature, defiled and impure.
The increase of afflictions obstructs the practitioner;
how could one suddenly grasp at them, claiming "this is right" or "that is wrong," thereby giving rise to various fetters and karmas that cause one to fall into the cycle of birth and death?
One perceives only suffering and its origin, but does not perceive the path and cessation.
Since one neither recognizes nor perceives the Four Noble Truths within volitional formations,
this lack of knowledge is termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
This continues up to old age and death.
However, because the causal conditions of ignorance persist, they are not extinguished.
Because they are not extinguished, one remains stubbornly attached and unable to relinquish them.
They remain only on this shore and do not reach the other shore.
As the Great Sūtra says:
"When a child was hungry, he took fruit from within dung."
When the wise rebuke them, they feel abashed and ashamed;
having lost the pure Dharma,
this is called being obstructed.
If, regarding any views, one gives rise to even a momentary thought and knows that they lack inherent nature, are truly impermanent, and have no master,
then through this overturning and destruction, there is no karma.
When there is no karma, there is no fruit;
this is called the Path.
Because of the Path, there is cessation.
If one realizes the Four Noble Truths, there will be no ignorance and no old age and death.
Because the chain of dependent origination is destroyed, one abandons all states of existence and reaches the further shore.
One should apply this principle to each and every moment of mind.
Passing through each and every faculty and passing through each and every object,
if the three obstructions arise, break them down to allow for penetration.
If these three types of nourishment are cultivated until they reach fulfillment,
then furthermore, the substance of seeing is itself emptiness, and the capacity for that seeing is also itself emptiness.
It is like the mind of an Arhat, which is still referred to as the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) though they are untainted (anāsrava).
I observe that as long as one has not yet attained the truth, how could one not be within the aggregates?
If one reckons the aggregates as real, this constitutes the karma and afflictions of birth and death;
if one does not recognize the four truths regarding the aggregates, this is precisely ignorance.
If one cherishes the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, one will be unable to relinquish it;
thus, employ the mind of emptiness to pass through each and every thought and each and every capacity.
Passing through each location,
if there are three obstructions, break them down to allow passage;
if there are three pathways, nurture them so that they reach fulfillment.
Then, skillfully overcoming the obstructions of views and thoughts,
one well penetrates three hundred *yojanas*.
Next, using horizontal weaving and vertical inspection to examine the penetration and obstruction from the perspective of the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness:
This is easy to understand.
Regarding the dharma of illness, the dharma of medicine, and the dharma of administering medicine,
for each respective dharma, each capacity, and each recipient:
Clearly discern the truths, conditions, and deliverances.
If the three obstructions arise, break them down to make them passable;
if the three paths exist, nurture them to bring them to fulfillment.
Thus, one passes through the obstruction of ignorance over a distance of four hundred *yojanas*.
Next, regarding the practitioner who employs horizontal weaving and vertical inspection to observe the Middle Way correctly:
concerning the true conditions of the dharma-nature of ignorance and so forth.
Each phenomenon has its own subject and its own object;
clearly recognize the truths, conditions, and deliverances.
If the three obstructions arise, break them down to allow for passage.
If one possesses the three penetrations and nurtures them to completion,
one will pass through the obstruction of ignorance for five hundred yojanas.
If one were to discuss penetration and obstruction in this manner:
In sequence, the first of the six stages is established.
It takes many kalpas for movement to pass through before it finally attains penetration.
As the Mahāyāna Sūtra says:
The srotāpanna reaches it after eighty thousand kalpas;
up to the pratyekabuddha, who reaches it after ten thousand kalpas;
and the bodhisattva reaches the stage of the first resolve after [ten thousand kalpas].
What benefit does this treatise offer to practitioners at the initial stage regarding the stages of the sages?
Furthermore, to discuss the general and the specific in terms of horizontal distinctions and their respective obstructions or permeability,
as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
There are bodhisattvas who, from the very first moment they resolve their minds [on enlightenment], are already in accord with sarvajñā (all-knowledge);
this is to be in accord with emptiness.
If they are not yet in accord at the outset, [they must cultivate it].
One should employ the means of the truths and conditions to examine each individual state of mind.
If there are three obstructions, break them down to allow for passage;
if there are three passages, nurture them to bring them to fulfillment.
It can travel three hundred yojanas.
Furthermore, it is said:
"There are bodhisattvas who, from the very moment they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], are able to sport with supernatural powers and purify buddha-fields."
This is the intent of emerging from the conventional.
If one cultivates the conventional upon first generating the bodhicitta,
one likewise employs the truths, objects, and perfections to examine each and every thought-moment.
The *Pusa chuyao jing* states that [the light] passes through four hundred yojanas.
It further says:

"There are bodhisattvas who, from the very first production of the thought of enlightenment (*prathamacittotpāda*), are able to sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and attain perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*)."
This is precisely the intended meaning.
If one cultivates the Middle Way from the initial arousal of the mind,
one likewise employs the truths, objects, and perfections to examine each and every moment of mind.
The "Breaking Obstructions and Sustaining Penetration" extends for five hundred *yojanas*.
According to this explanation,
although one attains the discourse on penetration and obstruction at the initial stage, the three dharmas remain distinct.
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra cites three analogies:
first, traveling on foot;
second, riding a horse.
Third is spiritual power (*abhijñā*).
One must know the passages and blockages along both the footpath and the horse-track;
spiritual power is unimpeded.
Obstructions cannot block it;
mountain walls are all void.
What passage could there be to choose?
First one contemplates the simile of walking;
next, the simile of horseback riding;
and finally, the simile of flying.
The threefold division of meaning is also not what is employed here.
If one discusses the three contemplations vertically,
two of the contemplations would be "open" (tong) in their respective stages and "obstructed" (se) when looking toward the higher stage.
If the latter contemplation excels the former, it is termed "penetration" (tōng); if it is inferior, it is termed "obstruction" (gé).

Regarding the three contemplations discussed horizontally, when they are categorized by their respective divisions, they are termed "penetration"; when they do not mutually encompass one another, they are termed "obstruction."
The depth or shallowness of dharmic characteristics may vary according to whether they are permeable or obstructed;
how much more so when one gives rise therein to ignorance, affliction, and obscuration?
For this reason, all are obstructed and there is no longer any permeability.
If one mind and three contemplations are such that their dharmic characteristics are mutually identical, this breaks through the obstructions and openings within the vertical;
the three contemplations and one mind break through the obstructions and openings within the horizontal.
Since emptiness is itself the three contemplations, it breaks through the three hundred obstructions and openings encountered when traversing mountain crags.
The "provisional" (jia) refers to the three contemplations that break through the obstructions and openings of the four hundred horse-riders;
the "middle" (zhong) refers to the three contemplations that break through the obstructions and openings of supernatural powers.
This is truly because the single mind can be identical with emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
All mountains, rivers, rocky cliffs, and the various hosts of Māras and heterodox paths are like empty space.
With single-mindedness and the threefold contemplation, one traverses them without obstruction;
one never descends from the high to the low, nor avoids the mountains to follow the valleys.
Wherever there are obstructions in the sense-field of touch, all are passed through without hindrance;
one is able to travel five hundred yojanas to reach the place of jewels.
This is called supernormal power (abhijñā).
Penetration is fundamentally opposed to obstruction.
Since all points of contact are like space, there is no longer any obstruction;
and where there is no obstruction, there is no penetration.
If one gives rise to the obscuration of ignorance regarding suffering and its origin within that which is neither obstructed nor unobstructed,
one will lose not only supernormal powers.
It also loses its momentum;
it can destroy that which is to be destroyed,
and the syllable becomes a non-syllable.
Just as those worms incidentally obtain the names of the "three contemplations," yet these worms do not know whether these are characters or not characters;
so it is with each and every dharma, each and every capacity, and each and every object.
All are simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle, fully possessing the truths, the conditions, and the perfections.
This is called being unobstructed yet unimpeded, illuminating both the open and the obstructed.
This is what is meant by the wise person’s recognition of letters and non-letters.
He is also called a skilled physician who knows both gain and loss,
one who clearly recognizes the openings and blockages within the gate of non-arising;
it is the same with respect to other Dharma gates as well.
This constitutes the initial mind having traversed five hundred *yojanas*.
One should clarify the meaning of the six stages of "immediacy" (*ji*), and so forth.

Question: Are the characters "penetration" (*tong*) and "obstruction" (*se*), as well as "gain" (*de*) and "loss" (*shi*), and "character" (*zi*) and "non-character" (*fei zi*), identical or different?
Answer: This is merely one meaning expressed in various ways;
there are also distinctions. Whether it is "penetrating" or "obstructed" depends on the level of understanding.
Gain and loss are defined by practice;
"letters" and "non-letters" are defined by teaching.
As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says:
To hear correctly, listen correctly, and discern correctly;
to understand correctly regarding conditions and to be able to awaken to them correctly—
knowing what is a syllable and what is not a syllable— is correct hearing and correct listening.
To know gain and loss is correct discernment and correct understanding of conditions;
to know penetration and obstruction is correct awakening and comprehension.
Although these distinctions exist, they equally manifest a single consistency.
Question:
If one blocks horizontally, does it remain open vertically?
If one blocks vertically, does it remain open horizontally?
If the horizontal is unobstructed while the vertical is obstructed, will it not pass through? If the vertical is unobstructed while the horizontal is obstructed, will it not pass through?
Answer: [It will.]
In the first case it is so, but in the second case it is not.
As for "so," since ignorance is identical to the views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa), for what reason would it not be a transverse obstruction?
If middling wisdom governs all things, why is it not pervasive and unobstructed? This is merely a provisional explanation.
If one explains it from a second perspective:
while it is obstructed and cannot block what is horizontal, it is unable to obstruct vertical pervasion.
The power of horizontal penetration is weak and cannot penetrate vertical obstructions;
vertical obstructions are deep and far-reaching and do not act as horizontal barriers.
Vertical penetration corresponds to its specific object and does not pass through horizontal obstructions.
Sixth, regarding the clarification of the suitability of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa):
there are four types of factors of enlightenment. The first is those belonging to their respective stages (prādeśika).
Second, mutual inclusion;
third, according to stages;
fourth, sequential generation.
First, regarding the "corresponding stage" (pratyutpanna-bhāga):
it is not necessarily the case that one must possess all factors to be able to attain the Path;
[the stages include] three, four, two, and five.
"Seven by one, eight by one;
this very moment is the Way.
Therefore it is said that one attains the Way by relying on the foundations of mindfulness."
It is also called the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
It is also called...
This is the Mahāyāna. Just as it is with the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), so it is with the other categories.
This constitutes the path-factors according to their respective divisions, rather than a harmonized synthesis.
Second, regarding the mutual inclusion [of factors]:
for example, a single dharma such as the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) includes all categories.
As the commentary on the *Śāstra* states:
Since the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) encompass the other factors of the path, and the other factors likewise encompass the foundations of mindfulness,
this constitutes their mutual inclusion; it is not a matter of equal distribution.
Third, regarding the stages: as in the case of the foundations of mindfulness, these correspond to their respective stages;
the right efforts correspond to the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata).
The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) constitute the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*); the five faculties (*indriya*) constitute the stage of patience (*kṣānti*);
and the five powers (*bala*) constitute the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The eightfold right path pertains to the stage of seeing the truths (darśanamārga),
while the seven factors of enlightenment pertain to the stage of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
This is a classification based on stages, and it is not a matter of balanced adjustment.
Regarding the arising of the four conditions:
for example, the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness can give rise to right effort,
and right effort gives rise to the bases of psychic power.
The bases of psychic power give rise to the five faculties;
the five faculties give rise to the five powers;
the five powers give rise to the seven factors of enlightenment.
The seven factors of enlightenment enter into the eightfold noble path;
this is called skillful adaptation.
Precept, concentration, wisdom, and so forth are all termed "right."
When the pure mind is constantly unified, one is able to perceive prajñā.
This constitutes the arising of signs and is also a state of equilibrium.
It is for this reason that this is required.
Although the preceding sections have refuted the pervasiveness of dharmas and examined the penetration and obstruction of consciousness,
if one does not harmonize the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas), how can one swiftly correspond with the true dharma?
The true dharma is called "outflow-free" (anāsrava).
The factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) are with-outflow (sāsrava).
That which is with-outflow can serve as the skillful means (upāya) for that which is without-outflow (anāsrava).
When skillful means miss their proper object, the true principle is difficult to realize.
Just as in the method of brewing wine, if the yeast and warmth are properly balanced,
water is transformed into wine;
yet if the mold and malt exceed their proper measure, the flavor will not be realized.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the dharmas for practicing the path.
The city of Nirvāṇa has three gates."
The three gates are the proximate causes, while the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) are the remote causes.
For this reason, it is necessary to harmonize and balance the factors of enlightenment.
Question:
The factors of the path (mārga-pakṣya-dharma) are the teachings of the Two Vehicles. What, then, is the path of a bodhisattva? Answer:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* rebukes this question, asking who could have uttered such words;
neither the Tripiṭaka nor the Mahāyāna makes such a statement.
How can it be claimed alone that this is a Hīnayāna teaching?
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"The factors of the path are good spiritual friends;
through them, one achieves perfect enlightenment."
The factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) are the site of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and are also the Mahāyāna.
As the Nirvāṇa-sūtra says:
"One who is able to cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path..."
To see the Buddha-nature immediately is called attaining the *amṛta* (the supreme essence).
The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the Bodhisattva’s *ratnolkā-dhāraṇī* (jewel-torch dhāraṇī)."
All such sutras clarify that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) pertain to the Path; how could they be exclusively of the Hīnayāna?
If a Mahāyāna sutra were to say that these thirty-seven factors are causes for nirvāṇa but not causes for Great Nirvāṇa (mahāparinirvāṇa), [it would contradict the truth].
Regarding the statement that "the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya factors conducive to enlightenment are the cause of this Great Nirvāṇa":
apart from the factors of the path (mārga-aṅga), there is no separate category of factors of the path.
Just as there is no fifth truth beyond the four truths, so too,
a single instance of suffering and its origin is like a speck of dust on a fingernail,
whereas the differentiated aspects of suffering and its origin are as infinite as the soil of the ten directions.
It is directly explained that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable factors of the thirty-seven aids to the path called the causes of *mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Why are they immeasurable? Because there are four kinds of the Truth of the Path.
Because there are sixteen gates.
Furthermore, regarding the factors of the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga-aṅga*): there are twenty-two in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and thirty-six in the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
In the first dhyāna, there are thirty-seven factors;
all these are the factors of the path with outflows (sāsrava), like milk.
The factors of the path according to the Tripiṭaka are like curd.
The factors of the path in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) are like fresh butter;
those in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao) are like matured butter; and those in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are like clarified butter (ghṛta).
The textual meaning of the Great Sūtra accords with this;
it is not that there are auxiliary dharmas existing separately outside of the *mārga-aṅgas*.
Some say that the thirty-seven factors are themselves the auxiliaries to the path.
Some say it is the Right Path;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that it is the Bodhisattva path.
This passage appears to be correct.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The factors of enlightenment and spiritual friends are the means by which one attains perfect awakening."
This passage seems to support [the former view].
Furthermore, if it were said that the thirty-seven factors are with outflows (sāsrava),
how could one say that the seven factors of enlightenment constitute the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)?
The Lotus Sūtra speaks of "the wealth of the untainted faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path. Why, then,
are the eightfold right paths placed before the seven factors of enlightenment?
This should be analyzed according to three propositions:
first, that all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are with outflows (*sāsrava*);
second, that they are all without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The third category is both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
As stated in the *Mahā-śāstra*:
"By practicing the Eightfold Noble Path, one attains the first wholesome five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that are with outflows."
The five aggregates of wholesome outflows are precisely the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata).
Since even prior to the stage of Heat one can cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path,
how is it that one cultivates it [at this stage]?
Initially receiving the Dharma from a teacher and binding the mind to mindful recollection is called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Diligently practicing in order to seek this Dharma is called right effort (*samyakpradhāna*).
Cultivating within a single mind is called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
The arising of the five wholesome faculties is called the faculties (*indriya*).
The growth of these faculties is called the powers (*bala*).
The discernment of the functions of the path is called the seven factors of enlightenment;
proceeding upon the secure path is called the eightfold noble path.
By being able to cultivate in this way, one attains the wholesome, out-flowing five aggregates.
When it is known that all these factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava),
they are precisely the factors practiced on the paths of seeing the truths (darśanamārga) and cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
It is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*);
this is the textual meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

Although it has been said from the past that one can cultivate the Eightfold Path, the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, and so forth within the tainted state, there has never been a scriptural proof for this.
However, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"If the eight [limbs] occur immediately after the seven factors of enlightenment,
they may be either contaminated (*sāsrava*) or uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)."
Why is this? Entering the vision of the truths by means of the Eightfold Noble Path is itself untainted (*anāsrava*).
